Statistical Modelling Methods: A Guide for the Social and Behavioural Sciences (2nd ed.)

Chapter 1: Foundations of Statistical Modelling Demonstrated with Simple Regression

David Flora

Setting Up

Importing Data

R can import lots of different data formats using different packages (e.g., SPSS, Excel, SAS, .csv, .txt, .dat). If you have your data in the same folder as your R project, you won’t need to specify the path to import your data. R will by default know that you’re choosing from that folder (this is called the “working directory”).

Setting Working Directory

You can also specify or change your working directory by inserting your desired path into the setwd() function. This path will be unique to your computer. Here is how I would set my working directory to my data folder:

#Set my working directory
setwd("C:/Users/dflora/OneDrive - York University/book/data")

Checking Working Directory

To check whether you have specified your preferred working directory, you can use the getwd() function:

getwd()

Importing Movie Data File

To import a .txt file, we can use the read.table() function in base R. There are different packages with functions that can read other file types into R (e.g., readxl::read_xlsx() for .xlsx, read.csv() for .csv, haven::read_sav() for .sav).

#Save movie.txt data file into an object called, "movie.profits"
#The "header = T" argument designates the first row as the column names
movie.profits <- read.table("movie.txt", header = T)
#We can then create a new dataframe object for data manipulation. We'll give this one a shorter name. 
movie <- movie.profits

Checking Structure of Data Frame

Before you can examine the statistical properties of your data, you should explore the structure of your dataframe object and your variables/variable types. Here we can make any necessary adjustments before we begin exploring the data.

#Check the structure of the object
str(movie)
## 'data.frame':    609 obs. of  7 variables:
##  $ year  : int  2012 2012 2012 2012 2012 2012 2012 2012 2012 2012 ...
##  $ title : chr  "Django Unchained" "Parental Guidance" "The Impossible" "Jack Reacher" ...
##  $ gross : num  162.8 77.3 19 80.1 67.5 ...
##  $ budget: num  100 25 40 60 35 40 250 35 15 65 ...
##  $ leng  : int  165 105 114 130 134 95 169 105 97 93 ...
##  $ score : int  88 18 81 61 51 38 64 4 75 12 ...
##  $ profit: num  62.8 52.3 -21 20.1 32.5 ...
#We see that each of the variables in our data frame are saved as the correct data type. If we wanted to change the type we could use the following functions: 

#Numeric
movie$title <- as.character(movie$title)
#Integer
movie$year <- as.integer(movie$year)
#Character
movie$gross <- as.numeric(movie$gross)

#Since each of these variables are already saved as their correct data types, the last three lines did not change anything. 
#This data file already includes a column for profit named "profit," but let's calculate our own and see if they're the same using the all.equal function

movie$profit2 <- movie$gross - movie$budget

all.equal(movie$profit, movie$profit2)
## [1] TRUE
#The function returned "TRUE"—the two profit columns are the same!
#Let's delete the second profit column now that we know it is redundant
movie<- subset(movie, select = -c(profit2))

Chapter 1 Textbook Content

A researcher obtains data for N = 606 movies released between 2008 and 2012. The researchers want to model the relationship between profit (in millions of USD) and reviews (“score”).

Research Example

Figure 1.1 R Code - Examining our data

Here we will visualize the distribution of profit. Since profit is a continuous variable, we can explore this through a boxplot and a histogram.

#Creating a boxplot of profit with a main label and a y label
boxplot(movie$profit, main="Boxplot of movie profits", ylab = "profit (millions $US)")

#Creating a histogram of profit with a main label and a y label
hist(movie$profit, main="Histogram of movie profits", xlab = "profit (millions $US)")
#Specify the axis range and ticks
axis(side=1,at=seq(-200,550,100))

Table 1.1 R Code - Descriptive Statistics

# Importing misty package for descriptive statistics
library(misty)
descript(movie, print= c('m','sd','min','p25','med','p75',
                                'max','iqr','skew','kurt'))
##  Descriptive Statistics
## 
##   Variable       M    SD     Min     p25     Med     p75     Max   IQR Skew  Kurt

##    budget    58.20 52.17    1.00   22.00   40.00   79.00  250.00 57.00 1.60  2.09

#Additional descriptive statistics (e.g., range) can be obtained through changing the print argument to print = "all".

Developing the Simple Regression Model

Figure 1.2 R Code - Correlation/Plot Between Profits and Review Score

We can visualize the relationship between reviews and profit with a scatterplot.

#Create a scatterplot of y ~ x with x- and y-axis labels.
plot(movie$profit ~ movie$score, xlab="review (% of positive reviews)", ylab="profit (millions $US)")

#Specify axis range and ticks.
axis(side=1,at=seq(0,100,10))

Product-moment Covariance and Pearson Correlation

#Sample product-moment covariance for profit and reviews
cov(movie$profit, movie$score)
## [1] 467.9771
#Pearson product-moment correlation for profit and reviews
cor.test(movie$profit, movie$score)
## 
##  Pearson's product-moment correlation
## 
## data:  movie$profit and movie$score
## t = 7.7479, df = 607, p-value = 3.942e-14
## alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.2259278 0.3706102
## sample estimates:
##       cor 
## 0.2999932

Alternate Scatterplot with LOESS Line

#Loading ggpubr package
library(ggpubr)

#Scatteprlots can also be created with the ggscatter function.
ggscatter(movie, y="profit", x="score", add = c("loess"), size = 1, shape=1)

Figure 1.3 R Code - Examining the Simple Model

We can assess the appropriateness of a linear model by plotting the relationship between the two variables and comparing the linear regression line with the non-parametric “LOWESS” (or “LOESS”) curve.

#Loading the car package
library(car)

#Create a scatterplot with a nonparametric LOWESS curve ("smooth" argument) and a regression line ("regLine=TRUE")
scatterplot(profit ~ score, boxplot=F, smooth=list(var=F, span=.2), regLine=T, data=movie,
            col="black", grid=F, xlab="review (% of positive reviews)",
            ylab="profit (millions $US)")

Simple linear regression: Model estimation

#Create the simple linear model using lm(y~x) and saving it as an object called "movieMod"
movieMod <- lm(profit ~ score, data=movie)

#Obtain model output
summary(movieMod)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = profit ~ score, data = movie)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -197.23  -29.34   -7.03   17.35  480.67 
## 
## Coefficients:
##              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept) -15.60263    4.88577  -3.193  0.00148 ** 
## score         0.70407    0.09087   7.748 3.94e-14 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 57.77 on 607 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:   0.09,  Adjusted R-squared:  0.0885 
## F-statistic: 60.03 on 1 and 607 DF,  p-value: 3.942e-14
#Obtain confidence intervals for estimates
confint(movieMod)
##                   2.5 %     97.5 %
## (Intercept) -25.1976889 -6.0075643
## score         0.5256094  0.8825353

Simple regression with a binary regressor

Simple regression models can also have a binary regressor (i.e. only two values). Here we will explore the relationship between year (2008 or 2009 only) and profit.

#Create data frame only containing movies released before 2010 (i.e., 2008 or 2009)
newer <- subset(movie, year < 2010)
#Create a "dummy variable" for year where 0=2008 and 1 = 2009.
newer$dum1 <- ifelse(newer$year==2008, 0, 1)

#Create scatter plot of relationship between year (dummy coded) and profit.
ggscatter(newer, y="profit", x="dum1", size = 1, shape=1)

#Add regression line to scatter plot with "add = "reg.line"" argument.
ggscatter(newer, y="profit", x="dum1", add = "reg.line", size = 1, shape=1)

Figure 1.4 R Code - Binary Regressor (movie year coded as binary variable)

#Create scatter plot of relationship between year (dummy coded) and profit.
plot(newer$dum1,newer$profit, xlab = "year (0 = 2008; 1 = 2009)", ylab="profit (millions $US)")

#Calculate mean profit for each year and put into object
means <- tapply(newer$profit, newer$dum1, mean)

#Add points to plot to represent mean profit for year.
points(0,means[1], col='black', lwd=8, pch=1); points(1,means[2], col='black', lwd=8, pch=1)

Distribution of residuals

Figure 1.5 R Code - Examining Residuals

Here we can create a quantile-quantile plot, or Q-Q plot, of the residuals of the model against the quantiles of a normal distribution.

#Create a Q-Q plot with a diagonal reference line.  
qqnorm(resid(movieMod), main="", ylab = "Residuals", xlab = "Theoretical normal quantiles"); qqline(resid(movieMod))

Homogeneity of variance

Figure 1.6 R Code - Examining Homoscedasticity

To assess homoscedasticity we can plot the reviews and against the model residuals and examine the spread of the data.

#Create a scatterplot of the relationship between model residuals and moview reviews. 
scatterplot(resid(movieMod) ~ score, boxplot=F, smooth=list(var=T, span=.2, style="lines", lty.smooth=1), regLine=F, data=movie,
            col="black", grid=F, xlab="review (% of positive reviews)",
            ylab="Residuals")
